mcqs.question: An app performs many small operations on the main thread, none individually slow, but collectively they exceed the ANR threshold while an input event is pending. Does this trigger an ANR?
options: No — ANRs only trigger from one single very slow operation, never from many small ones added together
Yes — the watchdog cares about total main-thread blocking time relative to a pending input event, regardless of whether that time comes from one slow call or many smaller ones
No — ANRs only apply to network calls, not general computation
Yes, but only if the app has fewer than 100MB of free memory at the time
mcqs.explanation: The ANR watchdog measures how long the main thread has been unable to process a pending input event or callback, regardless of whether that blocking time comes from a single long call or an accumulation of many smaller ones — both produce the same effect on responsiveness and can trigger the same watchdog.

mcqs.question: An anonymous inner class defined inside an Activity is registered with a long-lived system service. Its own code never explicitly references the Activity. Can it still leak the Activity?
options: No — since the code never mentions the Activity, there's no way for a reference to exist
Only if the inner class is declared as static
Yes — a non-static inner class (or anonymous class/lambda) implicitly holds a hidden reference to its enclosing instance regardless of whether its visible code mentions it
Only if the Activity itself explicitly passes a reference to the inner class's constructor
mcqs.explanation: Non-static inner classes, anonymous classes, and lambdas capture an implicit reference to their enclosing instance at the language level — this happens whether or not the class's visible code appears to reference the outer object, which is exactly why this leak pattern is easy to miss in a code review that only looks for explicit references.

mcqs.question: Given a choice between an explicit unregister call in onDestroy and wrapping a listener reference in a WeakReference, which is generally preferable when you can guarantee the unregister call will happen?
options: The explicit unregister call, because it deterministically breaks the reference at a known point rather than depending on garbage collector timing
The WeakReference, because it requires no additional lifecycle code
Both approaches are functionally identical in every respect
Neither — the only correct fix is switching to a static nested class
mcqs.explanation: An explicit unregister call breaks the reference deterministically at a known moment, while a WeakReference only allows garbage collection eventually, at a time the GC decides — when you can guarantee an unregister call will run, it's the more reliable and immediate fix; WeakReference is the fallback when you genuinely can't guarantee that.

mcqs.question: Leak-detection tooling flags an object that's still alive well after it was expected to be garbage collected. What distinguishes an actual leak from a legitimate long-lived cache?
options: Any object flagged by leak-detection tooling is automatically a bug that must be fixed
The only distinguishing factor is how much memory the object consumes
Caches are never flagged by leak-detection tooling, so any flag is definitely a leak

Whether the reference was held intentionally and is bounded (a capped cache with eviction) versus unintentional and unbounded, and specifically whether it's an Activity/View/Context reference rather than deliberately cached data
mcqs.explanation: The key questions are intent and boundedness — a deliberately maintained, size-capped cache holding data is a legitimate design choice even though it also lives longer than a single screen, while an unintended, unbounded reference to an Activity or View with no purpose behind it is the actual leak signature tooling is built to catch.

mcqs.question: A code reviewer scans an anonymous Runnable posted with a long delay via Handler, and sees no explicit mention of the enclosing Activity in its body. Should they conclude it's safe from leaking the Activity?
options: Yes — if the code doesn't mention the Activity by name, there's no reference to worry about

No — the implicit capture of the enclosing instance happens at the language level and isn't visible in the class's textual code, so a review based only on visible references will miss this leak pattern
Yes, but only for Runnables specifically; other listener types are always safe
No, but only if the delay is longer than 60 seconds
mcqs.explanation: The implicit reference to the enclosing instance is compiler-generated and invisible in the class's source text — a review looking only for explicit mentions of the Activity will not catch this, which is exactly why anonymous/inner classes handed to long-lived holders should be treated as leak candidates by default, regardless of what their visible code appears to reference.

mcqs.question: Why does a missing unregister call for a listener registered in onCreate often go unnoticed during normal testing, unlike a missing registration call?
options: Missing unregister calls always cause an immediate crash, making them easy to spot
Testing tools automatically detect missing unregister calls, making this a non-issue in practice
Unregister calls are optional by design and never required

A missing registration call breaks the feature immediately and visibly, while a missing unregister call produces no functional symptom at all — the feature keeps working normally, and the only consequence is an invisible, slowly-accumulating leak
mcqs.explanation: Skipping registration breaks the feature outright, which testing catches immediately — skipping unregistration leaves the feature working exactly the same, with the only consequence being a leak that accumulates silently and surfaces much later as an unrelated-looking crash, making it far easier to miss without a deliberate habit of pairing every registration with its counterpart.
